Source: Hermann Jacobi's 1884 translation of the Kalpa Sutra, drawing on both the 'Life of Mahavira' (Lecture 5, the account of Mahavira's death and Indrabhuti Gautama's attainment of Kevala) and the 'List of the Sthaviras' (which records Indrabhuti Gautama's standing among Mahavira's eleven Ganadharas), fetched directly from the sacred-texts.com etext. Gautama Swami is referred to in the source text by his personal name, Indrabhuti, of the Gautama gotra -- the gotra name by which he is popularly known today.

content.text: The Kalpa Sutra records that 'the oldest monk of the Venerable Ascetic Mahavira was Indrabhuti of the Gautama gotra, who instructed five hundred Shramanas' -- the senior-most of Mahavira's eleven Ganadharas (chief disciples), among whom two of his own brothers, Agnibhuti and Vayubhuti, also of the Gautama gotra, likewise led five hundred disciples each.
content.source_name: Jaina Sutras, Part I (Sacred Books of the East, Vol. 22), 'Kalpa Sutra: Life of Mahavira' and 'List of the Sthaviras', translated by Hermann Jacobi (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1884)

content.text: Of Indrabhuti Gautama and his ten fellow Ganadharas, the text records: 'All these eleven Ganadharas of the Venerable Ascetic Mahavira... knew the twelve Angas, the fourteen Purvas, and the whole Siddhanta of the Ganins' -- complete mastery of Mahavira's teaching, entrusted to them directly by their master.
content.source_name: Jaina Sutras, Part I (Sacred Books of the East, Vol. 22), 'Kalpa Sutra: Life of Mahavira' and 'List of the Sthaviras', translated by Hermann Jacobi (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1884)

content.text: Despite being the senior-most and most learned of Mahavira's disciples, Indrabhuti Gautama had not, while his master lived, attained Kevala (omniscience) -- Jacobi's translation records that this was owing to his own deep personal love for Mahavira, an attachment which, however devoted, was itself a bond the tradition holds must finally be cut for liberation.
content.source_name: Jaina Sutras, Part I (Sacred Books of the East, Vol. 22), 'Kalpa Sutra: Life of Mahavira' and 'List of the Sthaviras', translated by Hermann Jacobi (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1884)

content.text: On the night that Mahavira died, the Kalpa Sutra records: 'his oldest disciple, the monk Indrabhuti of the Gautama gotra, cut asunder the tie of friendship which he had for his master, and obtained the highest knowledge and intuition, called Kevala, which is infinite, supreme, unobstructed, unimpeded, complete, and full.' Only in that moment of profound loss did he attain the omniscience his own attachment had held back.
content.source_name: Jaina Sutras, Part I (Sacred Books of the East, Vol. 22), 'Kalpa Sutra: Life of Mahavira' and 'List of the Sthaviras', translated by Hermann Jacobi (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1884)

content.text: Jacobi's note on this episode explains the traditional understanding: 'Being aware that love had no place in one who is free from passion, he suppressed his friendship for his teacher and became a Kevalin' -- a teaching that even the purest devotion to a master, if it remains personal attachment, is itself among the last bonds to be released on the path to liberation.
content.source_name: Jaina Sutras, Part I (Sacred Books of the East, Vol. 22), 'Kalpa Sutra: Life of Mahavira' and 'List of the Sthaviras', translated by Hermann Jacobi (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1884)

content.text: In the account of Mahavira's final community, the Kalpa Sutra records 'an excellent community of fourteen thousand Shramanas with Indrabhuti at their head' -- naming Gautama as literally the head of Mahavira's entire monastic order among the tens of thousands of monks, nuns, and lay followers left behind.
content.source_name: Jaina Sutras, Part I (Sacred Books of the East, Vol. 22), 'Kalpa Sutra: Life of Mahavira' and 'List of the Sthaviras', translated by Hermann Jacobi (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1884)

content.text: Gautama lived twelve years after Mahavira's death, dying at ninety-two after fifty years as a monk. Yet the Kalpa Sutra notes that it was not through Gautama but through his younger colleague, Arya Sudharman, that the continuing line of teachers passed down to later generations: 'The Nirgrantha Shramanas of the present time are all (spiritual) descendants of the monk Arya Sudharman, the rest of the Ganadharas left no descendants' -- Gautama's own line, despite his seniority and devotion, was not the one the tradition continued through.
content.source_name: Jaina Sutras, Part I (Sacred Books of the East, Vol. 22), 'Kalpa Sutra: Life of Mahavira' and 'List of the Sthaviras', translated by Hermann Jacobi (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1884)
